overview: Two sex-linked inheritance patterns for genes on the X chromosome, differing in whether one or two copies are needed in females.
genZNote: X-linked recessive: sons get the short end of the stick. X-linked dominant: doesn't discriminate as much.

aspects.label: Expression in Females
aspects.valueA: A single copy on one X chromosome is enough to show the trait.
aspects.valueB: Requires both X chromosomes to carry the allele (homozygous) to show the trait.

aspects.label: Effect in Males
aspects.valueA: Males (XY) express the trait with just one copy, often more severely.
aspects.valueB: Males (XY) express the trait with just one copy, since they have no second X to mask it.

aspects.label: Father-to-Son Transmission
aspects.valueA: An affected father passes it to all daughters, no sons (since sons get his Y).
aspects.valueB: An affected father cannot pass it to his sons for the same reason — only to daughters (as carriers).

overlay.examHighYieldNote: A key NEET pedigree trick: X-linked traits are never passed from father to son directly, in either dominant or recessive form.
overlay.memoryTrick: X-linked recessive hits more males because they have only one X to 'fail'.
overlay.commonMisconception: X-linked recessive disorders are not more common in females — the opposite is generally true because males have no second X to compensate.
